newsitem.title: USA: Boeing CEO says Pentagon "very positive" on merger.
newsitem.headline: Boeing CEO says Pentagon "very positive" on merger.

text.p: Boeing Co. Chief Executive Officer Phil Condit said Tuesday the initial response from Pentagon officials to the company's planned merger with rival McDonnell Douglas Corp. had been "very, very positive."

At a news conference in Seattle, Condit also indicated that a separate organization within the merged company might be formed to centralize its commercial space operations, which he regarded as crucial to growth.
Condit said he had held general discussions with Pentagon brass Monday after announcing Boeing's plan to buy its longtime rival for about $14 billion in stock.
"This is just the very beginning of the formal process," Condit said. "Overall the reaction has been very, very positive."
A Defense Department spokesman said mergers like the one between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas made sense so long as competition continues.

"The department recognizes that consolidation of the defense industry is both inevitable and necessary as the defense budget has declined," Capt. Mike Doubleday said at a news briefing. "Consolidating and restructuring make good sense, as long as we continue to have competition."

Condit, dressed casually in a denim shirt and sweater after a flight from the East Coast, acknowledged that he would face a tough challenge in integrating workers from the very different cultures of Boeing, McDonnell Douglas and the just-acquired space and defense operations of Rockwell International Corp.

"It is a constant challenge to make sure people see the advantage of working together," Condit said. "We've spent years thinking about them as the competitor, and now you sort of have to turn your head and say gosh, I really like C-17s."
Boeing aggressively marketed its 747 jumbo jet for military airlift needs when McDonnell Douglas' C-17 program was in trouble with the Pentagon over cost and performance issues.

Condit said the merger would give Boeing a new critical mass in space operations, with its partly owned Sea Launch Co. and the space operations of McDonnell Douglas and Rockwell, all located in southern California.
He said a transition team would be formed in early January and one of the issues it would look at was whether it made sense to form a separate California-based space organization.
"Space is a big and growing business, particularly commercial space," Condit said. "Right now today there are more payloads than there are launchers. That's the kind of market you like to be in."

Condit said that after three years of on-and-off negotiations, the deal came together quickly after he called McDonnell Douglas Chief Executive Officer Harry Stonecipher Dec. 6 and invited him to Seattle.
Over coffee at breakfast Dec. 10, the two hammered out the basics of the deal, which was approved by directors of the two companies Dec. 14.
Condit said he was spurred to act in part over fear that the McDonnell Douglas was about to bid for Hughes Electronics, which would have made a Boeing merger too costly.
Under the merger agreement neither company can make any unapproved acquisitions while their merger is pending, meaning that McDonnell Douglas is out of the bidding for Hughes, Condit said.
